claims.text: Stand in a split stance holding one dumbbell in both hands, both hands wrapped around the handle.

quotes.text: Stand in a split-stance position holding a dumbbell with both hands and wrap both hands around the dumbbell handle.

claims.text: Another way: both hands on the inside surface of the plate.

quotes.text: Hold the weight overhead by grasping the inside dumbbell plate surface with both hands, or by grasping both handles of the kettlebell.

claims.text: Brace the torso, pull the shoulders down and back, and keep the head and neck in line with the spine throughout.

quotes.text: Stiffen your torso by contracting your abdominal/core muscles ("bracing"), and depress and retract your scapulae (pull your shoulders down and back), maintaining this position throughout the exercise.
Your head and neck should be aligned with your spine.

claims.text: Top position: arms vertical, elbows pointing forward and not completely locked, the dumbbell directly over the head.

quotes.text: Exhale and slowly press the dumbbell overhead, extending your elbows until your arms are vertical to the floor, elbows pointing forward, but not completely locked.
The dumbbell should be positioned directly over your head with your palms facing upwards and the dumbbell hanging vertically or angled slightly.

claims.text: Lower the dumbbell slowly behind the head without moving the upper arms; stop at about a 90-degree elbow bend or when the upper arms start to move back, and do not touch the back of the head.

quotes.text: Inhale and allow the weight to slowly bend your elbows, lowering the dumbbell behind your head in a controlled manner without moving your upper arms.
Continue lowering the dumbbell until your elbows reach a 90 degree bend or until your upper arms begin to move backwards. Be sure to avoid making contact with the back of your head.

claims.text: Keep the upper arms vertical and the elbows shoulder-width apart for the whole set.

quotes.text: Attempt to keep your upper arms vertical to the floor throughout the exercise and your elbows shoulder-width apart.

claims.text: Keep the head, torso, upper arms, wrists and feet still; only the elbows move.

quotes.text: Maintain your balance and avoid changing the position of your head, torso, upper arms, wrists and feet.

claims.text: Getting the weight into position is sometimes the hardest part; use a weight you can get to the start position safely.

quotes.text: Depending on what type of resistance you use (dumbbell, kettlebell, band, etc.), sometimes the most difficult part is getting the weight into position. Use a weight that allows you to get to the starting position safely.

claims.text: If the weight is too heavy or you are tired you may arch the back, which strains the back and shoulder joints.

quotes.text: If the weight is too heavy or you’re fatigued, you may be tempted to arch your back, which can increase the strain on your back and shoulder joints.
Keep the speed of movement relatively slow, and avoid momentum to focus on your form.

claims.text: It can also be done seated on a bench with back support.

quotes.text: Sit on a bench with back support or stand with feet shoulder-width apart, core engaged.

claims.text: Listed common mistakes: flaring the elbows outward, swinging the weight with momentum, arching the lower back and locking the elbows at the top.

quotes.text: Flaring elbows outward
Using momentum to swing weight
Arching lower back
Locking elbows at top

claims.text: A way out: a spotter is not usually needed, but for heavy sets one can help by supporting the elbows.

quotes.text: Spotting not typically required; assist by supporting elbows if needed for heavy sets.

claims.text: In an EMG study of the overhead dumbbell extension (21 resistance-trained men, one to two reps at 40% of a maximal isometric effort), the triceps long and lateral heads worked, most in the first and middle parts of the lift; the lowering phase needed less activity than the lift.

quotes.text: The long and lateral heads electromyographic signals were acquired from 21 resistance-trained men. One to two maximal repetitions of each exercise was performed with a 40% load of a maximal voluntary isometric contraction test.
Eccentric phase elicited less muscular activity than concentric in both exercises.
Concentric contraction presented the same pattern during OD (long and lateral heads) and LD (lateral head). Initial and middle intervals elicited higher muscle activity than final interval.

claims.text: Across all weight training (not this exercise specifically), the most common way people were hurt badly enough for an emergency department was a weight dropping on them, and 90% of injuries involved free weights.

quotes.text: The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%). A large number of injuries occurred with free weights (90.4%).

claims.text: Triceps tendon ruptures are rare; they often follow a forceful lowering (eccentric) contraction or lifting against resistance (not specific to this exercise).

quotes.text: Triceps tendon ruptures (TTRs) are rare and often occur as a result of falling on an outstretched hand, forceful eccentric contraction, direct trauma to the elbow, or lifting against resistance.

claims.text: Load progression: add 2-10% load once you can do one or two reps more than the target number.

quotes.text: When training at a specific RM load, it is recommended that 2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number.

claims.text: Tempo (up = pressing to straight arms, down = lowering): lower slowly and under control. Healthline asks to hold the fully extended position for a moment, right after the press, and gives no seconds, so the 1 s pause is a drawing convention (LR-33). ACSM's moderate 1-2 s each way is stated for advanced training (LR-15). Motra lists a tempo of "3-1-1" without saying which digit is which phase (WEAK); read as lowering-pause-lifting it gives 3 s down, a 1 s pause at the bottom and 1 s up. Motra's "Squeeze triceps at top." gives no pause or seconds. Breathe in on the way down and out on the way up.

quotes.text: at a moderate contraction velocity (1-2 s CON; 1-2 s ECC)
Inhale and allow the weight to slowly bend your elbows, lowering the dumbbell behind your head in a controlled manner without moving your upper arms.
Exhale and slowly press the dumbbell overhead, extending your elbows until your arms are vertical to the floor, elbows pointing forward, but not completely locked.
Squeeze triceps at top.
Then, at the lowest point, straighten your elbows and extend the weight back overhead. Hold the fully extended position for a moment, then repeat.

claims.text: Motra lists elbow joint pain under 'When to Avoid' for this exercise. Used for the elbow row's stop line (R-LB5-2).

quotes.text: Elbow joint pain

plate.viewWhy: The elbow bends front-to-back behind the head, and vertical upper arms (c6), the 90-degree stop (c5), the dumbbell clearing the head (c5) and a back arch (c9) all read side-on. Elbow flare (c12) is sideways. Census view is side.
plate.equipment: One dumbbell held vertically in both hands (census: dumbbell axis parameter). Standing split stance on the floor line (c1).
plate.start: Top position: split stance (c1), torso braced, shoulders down and back, head in line with the spine (c3); arms vertical, elbows pointing forward and not locked, dumbbell hanging vertically over the head (c4).
plate.end: Bottom position: elbows bent to about 90 degrees with the dumbbell behind, not touching, the head (c5); upper arms still vertical, elbows shoulder-width (c6); torso unchanged (c7).

checkpoints.label: Arms vertical
checkpoints.what: Upper arms stay vertical and still. Only the elbows bend.

checkpoints.label: Braced torso
checkpoints.what: Core braced, shoulders down and back, head in line with the spine.

checkpoints.label: Stop at 90°
checkpoints.what: Lower to about a right angle, clear of the back of the head.

mistake.what: Back arching as the dumbbell is pressed up.
mistake.why: Healthline says that when the weight is too heavy or you are tired you may be tempted to arch the back, which can increase the strain on the back and shoulder joints (c9). Motra lists it among the common mistakes (c12).
mistake.rankNote: No source measures how often each fault happens. LR-31 step 2: arching the back (c9). Step 1 set aside: Motra's "Spotting not typically required" is about spotting; Alves's "two commonly prescribed elbow extension exercises" is about the exercise, not a fault; Healthline's "The most common way to perform this exercise is using a dumbbell", "the long head tends to be most active" and "sometimes the most difficult part is getting the weight into position" are about equipment, a muscle's activity ('tend' is not a frequency word) and getting into position; Kerr's "The most common mechanism of injury was weights dropping on the person (65.5%)." (c15), "the most commonly injured body parts" and "The most common diagnosis was sprain/strain" are about all weight training; Gaviria's "Triceps tendon ruptures (TTRs) are rare and often occur as a result of falling on an outstretched hand, forceful eccentric contraction, direct trauma to the elbow, or lifting against resistance." (c16) is about ruptures in general, and forceful lowering is seen only as speed; Gaviria's "TTRs are most commonly seen in middle-aged men, football players, and weightlifters." says who gets ruptures, not that a fault of this exercise happens often; Motra's 'Common Mistakes' heading is a heading. Step 2: the arch is the only candidate a quote ties to harm (Healthline: "you may be tempted to arch your back, which can increase the strain on your back and shoulder joints"), and it is on Motra's list ("Arching lower back"). Motra's other items, "Flaring elbows outward", "Using momentum to swing weight" and "Locking elbows at top", and Healthline's "avoid momentum to focus on your form" name no harm. Motra's 'When to Avoid' items ("Elbow joint pain", "Recent rotator cuff injury") are conditions, not faults. The head's pick (the arch drawn, the flare called first) is replaced by step 2: the arch is the top fault and drawable is true, because the side view shows the back arch. handlingMistakes already has it first.

tempo.text: Pause 1 (LR-33): Healthline's "Hold the fully extended position for a moment, then repeat." (c18) asks for a pause right after the press and gives no seconds, so the 1 s is a drawing convention (WEAK); Motra's "Squeeze triceps at top." gives no pause or seconds. Motra's "3-1-1" (c18, WEAK: the page does not define the digit order, R-PB-3), read as lowering-pause-lifting, names a 1 s pause at the bottom, which is not this field. It would also give 3 s down; the card keeps 2 s down (ACSM, stated for advanced training, WEAK, LR-15; ACE's "slowly" gives no seconds) and lists the 3 s on the PR for a ruling (R-LB2-1). Up 1 s sits inside both.

plate.variantLine: Drawn standing in a split stance (ACE, anchor). A seated version on a bench with back support is also used (c11); the technique claims hold for both.

grip.type: One dumbbell held vertically in both hands, both hands wrapped around the handle (ACE).
grip.width: Both hands together on the handle.
grip.handContact: Both hands around the handle, palms facing up; the dumbbell hangs vertically over the head at the top (c1, c4).
grip.gripNote: Healthline's hold on the inside of the plate (c2) is not offered: it is thumbless, and content.md 5.2 allows no thumbless option for a free weight over the body.

setup.step: Pick a dumbbell you can get overhead safely.
Stand in a split stance, or sit on a back-supported bench.
Wrap both hands around the handle.
Brace, shoulders down and back, head in line with your spine.
Start with arms vertical, dumbbell over your head, elbows forward, not locked.

posture.point: Upper arms vertical and still, elbows shoulder-width apart, no flaring.
For heavy sets, a spotter can help by supporting your elbows.
Lower slowly behind your head to about 90°, without touching it.
Torso braced. Don't arch your back.
Head, torso, wrists and feet stay still.

handlingMistakes.fix: Brace. If the back still arches, use a lighter dumbbell.
Keep upper arms vertical, elbows shoulder-width. Stop lowering if they move.

rows.means: The triceps are doing the work.

rows.fix: Brace and use a lighter dumbbell.

rows.means: Fault: arching the back under a heavy weight.

rows.fix: Stop the set. Don't train through the pain.
rows.fixNote: The stop line rests on c19 (Motra, 'When to Avoid': "Elbow joint pain", WEAK; R-LB5-2); c16 covers the rupture and its usual cause (not specific to this exercise). The shared elbow box carries the referral (LR-27 R5).

risks.risk: Across weight training, dropped weights are the most common way people get badly hurt.
risks.riskNote: Kerr 2010's "most common mechanism" covers all weight training, so the line says so (dumbbell_biceps_curl's wording, LB2). Wrapping both hands round the handle (setup[2], c1), keeping the dumbbell clear of the head (posture[2], c5) and a weight you can get overhead safely (setup[0], c8) are shown in their own lines.

risks.risk: Triceps tendon rupture (rare), often from forceful lowering or lifting against resistance.
risks.riskNote: Back arching under a heavy weight (c9) left the risks list to make room for the separate progression line; it stays as the plate mistake, in handlingMistakes, posture and the back and shoulder feel rows.

risks.risk: Beat target by one or two reps? Add 2 to 10 percent.

zooms.right: Both hands wrapped round the handle, dumbbell hanging vertically.
zooms.wrong: Hands not wrapped round the handle.
zooms.wrongNote: The wrong drawing is the inverse of c1 (both hands wrapped around the handle); no source describes it directly.

zooms.right: Upper arms vertical, dumbbell clear of the head at 90°.
zooms.wrong: Upper arms dropped back, dumbbell touching the head.

libraryDiff.why: triceps primary matches exercises.json (c14). No secondary muscle is listed there. Motra's muscle breakdown rates Shoulders 4/10 (anterior delts), Forearms 3/10 (flexors) and Abs 2/10; not added, because it is a single coach source with unexplained ratings and no other source read names them.

gaps.why: No read source describes the kick-up, pressing it up from the thigh or seat, or setting it down (verify/g4.md item 2; LR-13).
